title: fullcycle tells the operator the build trees were not rebuilt after build all has already promoted the pair
body:
Found in Intent on 2026-09-15, in a real `devbin fullcycle --force` run whose `test rust` phase failed after `build all` had already promoted the pair. Read from Intent's vendored `bin/.devbin/lib/cmd/fullcycle`, which is byte-identical to this repository's `lib/cmd/fullcycle` at `6da4c81`. Not reproduced in a throwaway clone: the evidence is the run's own log and the branch's code.

The run's phase lines, from Intent's `tmp/fullcycle/20260915-1448-43.FULLCYC.out`:

    phase: clean rust           2s  rc=0
    ==> promoting the verified pair into the shared path
    phase: build all         2m05s  rc=0
    phase: test rust         2m59s  rc=101
    STOPPING: test rust failed. The remaining phases were NOT run.

    THE BUILD TREES WERE ALREADY REMOVED AND HAVE NOT BEEN REBUILT.
    Anything on PATH resolving through target/release/ is now dangling.
    Rebuild before doing anything else: bin/devbin build all

**Every line after `STOPPING` is false for this run.** `build all` had verified and promoted the pair two minutes earlier, `intent --version` named the commit the cycle built when it was measured after the run, and the daemon had restarted onto the new binary. Nothing on PATH was dangling.

## Why

`lib/cmd/fullcycle:379-394`: `cleaned` is set when `clean rust` passes, and the warning prints whenever `cleaned` is set and any later phase fails. The comment above the branch names the case it exists for -- _a build that fails after the delete leaves the estate with no release artefacts_ -- and the condition never asks whether a build has succeeded since the delete. With the phase list at `:89-93` (`clean rust`, `build all`, `test rust`), the test phase is the one failure that can follow a successful build, and there the warning is always false.

## Why it is worth an issue

This message is what an operator reads at the moment a cycle has gone wrong, and it tells them the machine is broken in a way it is not: every tool resolving through `target/release/` is said to be dangling, with a rebuild named as the thing to do before anything else. A redundant remedy costs a build. A false one teaches the reader to discount the same branch on the day a build really has failed after the delete, which is the day it is true.

## Shape of a fix, not a ruling

Track the rebuild the way the clean is tracked -- a flag set when `build all` passes -- and print the dangling warning only when the clean passed and no build has passed since. After a later failure, say what is true instead: the build trees were rebuilt and promoted, and the failure is in the phase named. Hold it with an arm per failing phase: a cycle whose test phase fails after a passing build prints no dangling warning, and one whose build phase fails after a passing clean still does.
